summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) operations. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers that pass the same video to many viewers at once need settings. This document defines a standard layout for those settings so management tools can handle them.

subtitle: A standard YANG schema for configuring MSDP peers and reading back their state and the Source-Active cache.

tldr.problem: Operators configure the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) differently on each vendor's router, which makes automated management hard.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8916 defines the ietf-msdp YANG module. It augments the routing model with global and per-peer configuration, read-only state and statistics, a Source-Active cache and actions to clear peers or cache entries.
tldr.outcome: Management tools using NETCONF or RESTCONF can configure and monitor MSDP the same way across implementations that support the module.

today: RFC 8916 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2020. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What the Model Covers
sections.content:
RFC 3618 defines the Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP). RFC 8916 adds a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage MSDP operations. The same model also exposes operational state data and statistics.

The model is meant to be used alongside other multicast YANG models such as the one for PIM, which are not covered in this document. It defines no protocol-specific notifications, but users can apply the subscription and push mechanisms of RFC 8639 and RFC 8641 to the data nodes it defines.

The model holds the basic parameters needed to run the protocol. Parameters that only some implementations offer are modeled as optional features, and the module can be extended.
sections.plainLanguage: MSDP is how multicast routers tell each other about live streams. This document is the standard settings form for those routers, plus a way to read back how they are doing.

sections.title: Module Structure and Placement
sections.content:
The module is named ietf-msdp. It imports and augments the ietf-routing model of RFC 8349, adding an msdp container under the control-plane protocol list. Both the configuration and the state parts of that routing model are augmented. The presence of the msdp container is expected to enable MSDP functionality.

The model follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA) of RFC 8342, so operational state sits in the same hierarchy as the matching configuration. Under msdp there are three parts: global settings, a list of peers, and a read-only sa-cache.

The module imports types and models for interfaces, IP, key chains, routing types and access control lists, which it uses to refer to interfaces, authentication keys and filter policies.
sections.plainLanguage: The model plugs into the routing settings that already exist. It has three drawers: settings for the whole router, a drawer for each neighbor, and a read-only notebook of streams the router has heard about.

sections.title: Configuration: Global and Per-Peer
sections.content:
MSDP operation needs configuration spread across several peers, and peers can be grouped in a mesh group. The configuration branch has global and peer parts.

Global settings include the interface used as the source of TCP connections, a default-peer list, the originating-rp interface, inbound and outbound sa-filter access lists, an sa-limit and a ttl-threshold. A default peer accepts all Source-Active (SA) messages. It is needed where MSDP peers do not coexist with BGP peers, because the Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF) check on SA messages would otherwise fail and no SA messages would be accepted.

Each peer is keyed by its IPv4 address and can carry authentication, an enabled flag, a description, a mesh-group name, an optional peer-as, its own SA filters and limit, and a timer container. An sa-limit of 0, or none, means no limit. The ttl-threshold is the maximum number of hops data packets can traverse before being dropped.

Optional features are filter-policy, peer-as-verification and peer-authentication. Systems that do not support them can leave them out.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell the router who its neighbors are, how many stream announcements to accept, and which ones to ignore. Neighbors can also be put in a club that shares announcements among themselves.

sections.title: Peer Authentication and Timers
sections.content:
MSDP runs over TCP, so the model includes connection parameters. The authentication container, available with the peer-authentication feature, lets an operator choose between two cases: a reference to a key chain (RFC 8177), or a direct key with a crypto-algorithm.

Only the md5 algorithm can be used for MSDP. When it is specified, MSDP control messages are secured by TCP MD5 signatures as described in RFCs 3618 and 5925, and both peers SHOULD be configured with the same algorithm for the connection to be established. When the algorithm is not configured, unauthenticated TCP is used.

The timer container holds three values in seconds: connect-retry-interval (default 30), holdtime-interval (default 75, range 3 to 65535) and keepalive-interval (default 60, range 1 to 65535). The keepalive interval must be smaller than the hold-time interval.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors can use a shared secret password to prove who they are. There are also timers, like how often to say "still here" and how long to wait before assuming a neighbor is gone.

sections.title: State, Statistics and the SA Cache
sections.content:
State data is read-only. Per peer it includes the session-state (disabled, inactive, listen, connecting or established), elapsed time, timer expiry values, whether the peer is a default peer and a reset count.

The statistics container holds a discontinuity time, an RPF failure count, input and output queue sizes, and counters for received and sent messages: keepalive, notification, SA message, SA response, SA request and total.

The sa-cache lists entries keyed by multicast group and source address. Each entry records the originating Rendezvous Point (RP), whether it is local, and state attributes such as up time, expiry, hold-down interval, the peer the entry was learned from and the RPF peer.
sections.plainLanguage: The router also keeps score. You can ask whether each neighbor is connected, how many messages went back and forth, and which streams it has heard about and from whom.

sections.title: Actions to Clear Peers and Cache Entries
sections.content:
The module defines YANG actions rather than notifications for resetting things. clear-peer clears the TCP connection to one peer, and clear-all-peers clears every peer's connection.

The clear action on the SA cache removes entries. Its optional input names a group and, optionally, a source address, plus an optional peer address and peer AS number. If no entry is given, all entries are cleared. If no peer address or AS is given, entries learned from all peers or all ASes are cleared.
sections.plainLanguage: There are reset buttons. One restarts the link to a single neighbor, one restarts all of them, and one wipes the notebook of known streams, either all of it or just certain pages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed with NETCONF or RESTCONF, with SSH and TLS as the mandatory-to-implement secure transports, and access can be limited with the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM). The RFC warns that writable nodes under msdp are sensitive: changes to global can delete default peers, rebuild connections or cause unexpected SA filtering, and changes to peers can allow unexpected peer establishment and SA learning.

Readable data is sensitive too. Disclosing peer information may lead to a forged connection attack, and the key field may leak the password. The clear actions can cause peer connections to be rebuilt or SA records to be deleted, so access to them should be controlled.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can change these settings can disrupt the network, and anyone who can read them might learn the secret password. So only trusted people should get access.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-msdp in the IETF XML Registry. It also registered the YANG module ietf-msdp with prefix msdp in the YANG Module Names registry, with this RFC as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The name of the settings form was written in an official list so nobody else uses the same name.
